title: Assign Elements to Groups with Constraints
statement:
You get two integer arrays: `groups`, where `groups[i]` is the size of group `i`, and `elements`. Each group is matched with one index of `elements`: group `i` may only take an index `j` for which `groups[i]` is a multiple of `elements[j]`, and among all such indexes it takes the smallest one. A group whose size no element divides gets `-1` instead.

Return the chosen indexes as an array with one entry per group, in the order of `groups`. The same index may serve any number of groups.
notes:
## Intuition

The direct way tries every element on every group, which is O(n·m) and up to 10^10 checks. Turn the question around: instead of asking which elements divide a size, let each element claim every size it divides, which are exactly its multiples. Sizes stop at the largest group size `M`, and a value `v` has only `M / v` multiples up to it, so walking the multiples of distinct values costs at most `M·(1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + …) ≈ M ln M`, like a sieve. If the elements claim sizes in index order and never overwrite a claim, every size ends up with the smallest index that divides it.

## Approach

1. Let `limit` be the largest group size and fill `owner[0..limit]` with -1. `owner[s]` will be the smallest index of an element dividing `s`.
2. Visit the elements in index order. Skip `value` if it exceeds `limit` (it divides no size), or if `owner[value]` is already set: then an earlier element divides `value`, so it also divides, and has already claimed, every multiple of `value`. This skip also covers repeated values.
3. Otherwise walk `multiple = value, 2·value, …` up to `limit` and claim every multiple whose `owner` is still -1.
4. Answer each group with `owner[size]`.

## Example 1, step by step

`groups = [8,4,3,2,4]`, `elements = [4,2]`, so `limit = 8`. Index 0 (value 4) claims sizes 4 and 8. Index 1 (value 2): `owner[2]` is still -1, so it walks 2, 4, 6 and 8, claiming 2 and 6 while 4 and 8 keep owner 0. Reading `owner` at 8, 4, 3, 2 and 4 gives `[0, 0, -1, 1, 0]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(M log M + n + m), where M is the largest group size: the walks over multiples form a harmonic sum, and every group and element is visited once more.
- Space: O(M) for `owner`.

## Pitfalls

- Never overwrite a claimed size: a later index with a smaller value (such as a 1 at the end) must not replace an earlier divisor.
- Without the skip, `elements = [1, 1, 1, …]` walks all M sizes once per copy, which is O(M·m).
- In Java or C, reading `owner[value]` for a value above `limit` is out of bounds, so test `value > limit` first.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `limit` | the largest group size |
| `owner` | `owner[s]`: smallest index of an element dividing `s`, or -1 |
| `j`, `value` | the current element's index and value |
| `multiple` | a multiple of `value` up to `limit` |
| `size` | the size of the group being answered |

narration.2: Only sizes up to the largest group can be asked about, so the table stops there.
narration.3: owner[s] will hold the smallest index of an element that divides s; -1 means no element yet.
narration.4: Visit the elements from the smallest index up, so the first claim on a size is always the right one.
narration.6: A value above every size divides none of them; and if value's own slot is taken, an earlier element divides value and so already owns all its multiples.
narration.7: Either way this element cannot win any group, so skip it.
narration.9: Walk the multiples of value up to limit: exactly the sizes that value divides.
narration.10: Only a size nobody has claimed yet takes this index; an earlier index always wins.
narration.11: Record j as the owner of this size.
narration.15: Each group's answer is the owner of its size, or -1 if no element divides it.
